claim: The ClpXP degradation machine consists of a hexameric AAA+ unfoldase (ClpX) and a pair of heptameric serine protease rings (ClpP).
source: The ClpXP degradation machine consists of a hexameric AAA+ unfoldase (ClpX) and a pair of heptameric serine protease rings (ClpP) that unfold, translocate, and subsequently degrade client proteins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ClpXP unfolds, translocates, and subsequently degrades client proteins.
source: The ClpXP degradation machine consists of a hexameric AAA+ unfoldase (ClpX) and a pair of heptameric serine protease rings (ClpP) that unfold, translocate, and subsequently degrade client proteins.
evidence: This functional description is stated in the abstract and supported by the degradation assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: ClpXP is an important target for drug development against infectious diseases.
source: ClpXP is an important target for drug development against infectious diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding various inhibitors.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of the substrate-bound ClpXP complex from Neisseria meningitidis were obtained at 2.3 to 3.3 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present cryo-EM structures of the substrate-bound ClpXP complex from Neisseria meningitidis at 2.3 to 3.3 Å resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the resolution values reported in the methods and results sections.

claim: Sequential hydrolysis of ATP is coupled to motions of ClpX loops that lead to directional substrate translocation.
source: The structures allow development of a model in which the sequential hydrolysis of ATP is coupled to motions of ClpX loops that lead to directional substrate translocation and ClpX rotation relative to ClpP.
evidence: This mechanistic model is derived from the structural data showing different conformations and nucleotide states.

claim: Sequential hydrolysis of ATP is coupled to ClpX rotation relative to ClpP.
source: The structures allow development of a model in which the sequential hydrolysis of ATP is coupled to motions of ClpX loops that lead to directional substrate translocation and ClpX rotation relative to ClpP.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis showing different IGF loop binding positions and ClpX orientations.

claim: AAA+ molecular machines generate translocating forces by a common mechanism.
source: Our data add to the growing body of evidence that AAA+ molecular machines generate translocating forces by a common mechanism.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the ClpXP structures with other AAA+ ATPase structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: Protein degradation plays a central role in cellular physiology, regulating the timing of cell division, controlling stress responses, and ensuring the timely removal of damaged or aberrantly folded proteins.
source: Protein degradation plays a central role in cellular physiology, regulating the timing of cell division, controlling stress responses, and ensuring the timely removal of damaged or aberrantly folded proteins (Olivares et al., 2016; Goldberg, 2003).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ClpXP system is central to protein degradation in bacteria and in mitochondria.
source: The ClpXP system is central to protein degradation in bacteria and in mitochondria, where it has recently emerged as a therapeutic target against malignancies (Ishizawa et al., 2019), and is a key regulator of cellular homeostasis, pathogenesis, and intracellular parasitism (Frees et al., 2014; Pickart and Cohen, 2004; Bhandari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: ClpXP has recently emerged as a therapeutic target against malignancies.
source: The ClpXP system is central to protein degradation in bacteria and in mitochondria, where it has recently emerged as a therapeutic target against malignancies (Ishizawa et al., 2019), and is a key regulator of cellular homeostasis, pathogenesis, and intracellular parasitism (Frees et al., 2014; Pickart and Cohen, 2004; Bhandari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ishizawa et al., 2019.

claim: ClpXP is a key regulator of cellular homeostasis, pathogenesis, and intracellular parasitism.
source: The ClpXP system is central to protein degradation in bacteria and in mitochondria, where it has recently emerged as a therapeutic target against malignancies (Ishizawa et al., 2019), and is a key regulator of cellular homeostasis, pathogenesis, and intracellular parasitism (Frees et al., 2014; Pickart and Cohen, 2004; Bhandari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frees et al., 2014; Pickart and Cohen, 2004; Bhandari et al., 2018.

claim: ClpXP serves as a model for understanding the structure and function of other ATP-dependant proteolytic systems.
source: It also serves as a model for understanding the structure and function of other ATP-dependant proteolytic systems.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for studying ClpXP.

claim: The ClpXP holoenzyme is composed of a hexameric AAA+ unfoldase (ClpX) and a tetradecameric serine protease consisting of two heptameric rings (ClpP).
source: The ClpXP holoenzyme is composed of a hexameric AAA+ (ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities) unfoldase (ClpX) and a tetradecameric serine protease consisting of two heptameric rings (ClpP).
evidence: This structural composition is stated in the introduction and confirmed by the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The ClpXP complex acts to unfold and degrade protein substrates.
source: Together, the ClpXP complex acts to unfold and degrade protein substrates (Figure 1A; Baker and Sauer, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ClpXP function is critical in many bacteria.
source: ClpXP function is critical in many bacteria, and consequently small molecules that disrupt either the protease (e.g. β-lactones [Böttcher and Sieber, 2008], phenyl esters (Hackl et al., 2015; Lakemeyer et al., 2019) or the AAA+ unfoldase (e.g. ecumicin (Gao et al., 2015), lassomycin (Gavrish et al., 2014), rufomycin (Choules et al., 2019), dihydrothiazepines (Fetzer et al., 2017), or mimic the interaction between the two (e.g. acyldepsipeptides [ADEPs] (Kirstein et al., 2009; Gersch et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2018) can kill cells, establishing ClpXP as a target for novel therapeutics against a range of different infectious diseases and cancers (Culp and Wright, 2017; Malik and Brötz-Oesterhelt, 2017; Raju et al., 2012; Goard and Schimmer, 2014; Wong and Houry, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing various inhibitors and their effects.

claim: Small molecules that disrupt ClpXP can kill bacterial cells.
source: ClpXP function is critical in many bacteria, and consequently small molecules that disrupt either the protease (e.g. β-lactones [Böttcher and Sieber, 2008], phenyl esters (Hackl et al., 2015; Lakemeyer et al., 2019) or the AAA+ unfoldase (e.g. ecumicin (Gao et al., 2015), lassomycin (Gavrish et al., 2014), rufomycin (Choules et al., 2019), dihydrothiazepines (Fetzer et al., 2017), or mimic the interaction between the two (e.g. acyldepsipeptides [ADEPs] (Kirstein et al., 2009; Gersch et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2018) can kill cells, establishing ClpXP as a target for novel therapeutics against a range of different infectious diseases and cancers (Culp and Wright, 2017; Malik and Brötz-Oesterhelt, 2017; Raju et al., 2012; Goard and Schimmer, 2014; Wong and Houry, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing various inhibitors.

claim: ClpP has a barrel-like structure with protease rings stacked coaxially to form an enclosed degradation chamber.
source: X-ray crystallographic studies of ClpP alone reveal a barrel-like structure with the protease rings stacked coaxially to form an enclosed degradation chamber, akin to the 20S proteasome (Förster et al., 2013; Kish-Trier and Hill, 2013), that sequesters the fourteen Ser-His-Asp catalytic triads (Wang et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallographic studies cited in the text.

claim: ClpP sequesters fourteen Ser-His-Asp catalytic triads.
source: X-ray crystallographic studies of ClpP alone reveal a barrel-like structure with the protease rings stacked coaxially to form an enclosed degradation chamber, akin to the 20S proteasome (Förster et al., 2013; Kish-Trier and Hill, 2013), that sequesters the fourteen Ser-His-Asp catalytic triads (Wang et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallographic studies cited in the text.

claim: One or two ClpX particles can bind co-axially to ClpP, creating a continuous central channel for substrates.
source: Early negative-stain electron microscopy showed that one or two ClpX particles can bind co-axially to ClpP, creating a continuous central channel for substrates from ClpX to the degradation chamber of ClpP (Ortega et al., 2002; Ortega et al., 2000; Kessel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on early negative-stain EM studies cited in the text.

claim: The axial entrances to the ClpP degradation chamber are gated by flexible N-terminal loops.
source: Biochemical and X-ray crystallographic studies show that the axial entrances to the degradation chamber are gated by flexible N-terminal loops of ClpP that open upon the binding of ClpX or ADEPs, allowing substrates into the degradation chamber (Lee et al., 2010; Li et al., 2010; Effantin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on biochemical and X-ray crystallographic studies cited in the text.

claim: ClpP N-terminal loops open upon the binding of ClpX or ADEPs, allowing substrates into the degradation chamber.
source: Biochemical and X-ray crystallographic studies show that the axial entrances to the degradation chamber are gated by flexible N-terminal loops of ClpP that open upon the binding of ClpX or ADEPs, allowing substrates into the degradation chamber (Lee et al., 2010; Li et al., 2010; Effantin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on biochemical and X-ray crystallographic studies cited in the text.

claim: Binding of ClpX and ClpP is mediated by loops containing an Ile/Leu-Gly-Phe motif (I/LGF loops) on ClpX that dock into hydrophobic pockets on the apical interfaces of ClpP subunit pairs.
source: Binding of ClpX and ClpP is mediated by loops containing an Ile/Leu-Gly-Phe motif (I/LGF loops) on ClpX that dock into hydrophobic pockets on the apical interfaces of ClpP subunit pairs (Kim et al., 2001; Joshi et al., 2004; Amor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on biochemical studies cited in the text.

claim: N-terminal loops on ClpP transiently interact with ClpX.
source: N-terminal loops on ClpP also transiently interact with ClpX (Joshi et al., 2004; Gribun et al., 2005; Jennings et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on biochemical studies cited in the text.

claim: ClpX uses energy released by ATP hydrolysis to create a pulling force that unravels folded protein domains for translocation into the degradation chamber of ClpP.
source: ClpX uses energy released by ATP hydrolysis to create a pulling force that unravels folded protein domains for translocation into the degradation chamber of ClpP (Baker and Sauer, 2012).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism cited from Baker and Sauer, 2012.

claim: ClpX unfolding activity relies on conserved loops including 'RKH' loops and 'pore loops'.
source: This unfolding activity relies on a series of conserved loops in ClpX. These loops include the 'RKH' loops that surround the ClpX entrance pore and recognize substrates for proteolysis (Martin et al., 2008a), and a pair of 'pore loops' in each protomer, termed pore-1 loop (GYVG in Neisseria meningitidis ClpX, NmClpX) and pore-2 loop (RDV in NmClpX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that line the axial channel of the ClpX ring (Martin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RKH loops surround the ClpX entrance pore and recognize substrates for proteolysis.
source: These loops include the 'RKH' loops that surround the ClpX entrance pore and recognize substrates for proteolysis (Martin et al., 2008a), and a pair of 'pore loops' in each protomer, termed pore-1 loop (GYVG in Neisseria meningitidis ClpX, NmClpX) and pore-2 loop (RDV in NmClpX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that line the axial channel of the ClpX ring (Martin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is based on Martin et al., 2008a and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pore loops line the axial channel of the ClpX ring.
source: These loops include the 'RKH' loops that surround the ClpX entrance pore and recognize substrates for proteolysis (Martin et al., 2008a), and a pair of 'pore loops' in each protomer, termed pore-1 loop (GYVG in Neisseria meningitidis ClpX, NmClpX) and pore-2 loop (RDV in NmClpX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that line the axial channel of the ClpX ring (Martin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is based on Martin et al., 2008b and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bulky aromatic and aliphatic side chains of the pore loops transmit the pulling force to the substrate, leading to its unfolding.
source: Bulky aromatic and aliphatic side chains of the pore loops transmit the pulling force to the substrate, leading to its unfolding.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the structural data showing pore loop-substrate interactions.

claim: The mechanism by which some AAA+ ATPases convert energy from ATP hydrolysis into a mechanical force that unfolds substrates was established recently.
source: The mechanism by which some AAA+ ATPases convert energy from ATP hydrolysis into a mechanical force that unfolds substrates was established recently (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017), and structures of ClpP and ClpX in isolation have been determined (Ishizawa et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016; Geiger et al., 2011; Glynn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on recent structural studies cited in the text.

claim: Structures of ClpP and ClpX in isolation have been determined.
source: The mechanism by which some AAA+ ATPases convert energy from ATP hydrolysis into a mechanical force that unfolds substrates was established recently (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017), and structures of ClpP and ClpX in isolation have been determined (Ishizawa et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016; Geiger et al., 2011; Glynn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on previous structural studies cited in the text.

claim: The absence of structures showing ClpXP in the process of unfolding substrate has prevented an understanding of the conformational changes necessary for substrate engagement, unfolding, and translocation.
source: However, the absence of structures showing ClpXP in the process of unfolding substrate has prevented an understanding of the conformational changes that are necessary for substrate engagement, unfolding, and translocation in this system.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: ClpXP must undergo hundreds of ATP hydrolysis events to unfold and degrade a single protein.
source: ClpXP must undergo hundreds of ATP hydrolysis events to unfold and degrade a single protein, likely via a process involving hydrolysis of one nucleotide at a time, but the lack of structural information for a ClpXP holoenzyme has limited understanding of how unfolding and degradation are coupled.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about ClpXP function.

claim: There is a symmetry mismatch between the pseudo-symmetric hexameric ClpX and the seven-fold symmetric ClpP.
source: For example, it is not clear how the symmetry mismatch (Bewley et al., 2006; Beuron et al., 1998; Majumder et al., 2019) between the pseudo-symmetric hexameric ClpX and the seven-fold symmetric ClpP affects both the binding and interaction of these two components.
evidence: This is stated as a known issue with citations to previous work.

claim: Degradation of GFP-SsrA by ClpXP is ATP-dependent.
source: ClpX, ClpP, and ATP were all necessary to degrade GFP-SsrA (Figure 1B), confirming that degradation of GFP-SsrA by ClpXP is ATP-dependent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the degradation assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The presence of MgATP is required for tight binding between ClpX and ClpP.
source: As shown below and in previous work (Joshi et al., 2004; Hersch et al., 2005; Grimaud et al., 1998; Jones et al., 1998), the presence of MgATP is required for tight binding between ClpX and ClpP.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work and confirmed by the SEC experiments.

claim: An E185Q Walker B mutant of NmClpX was used to slow ATP hydrolysis and prolong the lifetime of the ClpXP complex.
source: Therefore, for further structural studies, an E185Q Walker B mutant of NmClpX (ClpX-WB) was used to slow ATP hydrolysis and prolong the lifetime of the ClpXP complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: ClpP behaves as an oligomeric species consistent with its tetradecameric architecture.
source: SEC was performed to probe the oligomeric state of each component and the formation of the holoenzyme, confirming that ClpP behaves as an oligomeric species, consistent with its well-known tetradecameric architecture (Figure 1C – blue trace).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ClpX-WB eluted as a hexamer in the presence of 2 mM MgATP.
source: ClpX-WB eluted as a hexamer in the presence of 2 mM MgATP (Figure 1C – green trace).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Incubation of ClpX-WB and ClpP in the presence of MgATP resulted in formation of singly and doubly capped ClpXP complexes.
source: Incubation of ClpX-WB and ClpP in the presence of MgATP resulted in a pair of higher molecular weight SEC peaks that contain both ClpX and ClpP (Figure 1C – red trace and SDS-PAGE gel insert), presumably corresponding to singly and doubly capped ClpXP complexes, showing that the N. meningitidis ClpX:ClpP complex can be readily reconstituted in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data and SDS-PAGE shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ClpX is positioned with an offset and is tilted relative to the seven-fold symmetry axis of ClpP.
source: Atomic models built into the cryo-EM maps showed that in both Conformations A and B, ClpX is positioned with an offset and is tilted relative to the seven-fold symmetry axis of ClpP (Figure 1D, Video 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: A continuous channel for substrate spans the ClpX and ClpP rings.
source: Nevertheless, a continuous channel for substrate spans the ClpX and ClpP rings.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: ClpP is in its active extended conformation.
source: ClpP is in its active extended conformation (Goodreid et al., 2016), and closely resembles a published ADEP-bound crystal structure with an all atom RMSD of 1.18 Å for the tetradecamer (pairwise comparison of the chains gives values from 1.12 to 1.22 Å with a standard deviation from the mean of 0.03 Å) (Goodreid et al., 2016).
evidence: This is determined by comparing the cryo-EM structure to a published crystal structure.

claim: No density was found for the zinc binding domains of ClpX in either conformation, likely due to their flexibility.
source: Even though the full-length constructs of ClpX included the zinc binding domains (residues 1–62), no density was found for these domains in either conformation, likely due to their flexibility.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps and explained by flexibility.

claim: Additional density along the axial channels of ClpX in Conformations A and B is likely from the GFP-SsrA substrate.
source: Conformations A and B of ClpX both contained additional density along their axial channels, adjacent to the pore loops, likely from the GFP-SsrA substrate that co-eluted with ClpXP from the SEC column (Figure 1E and F - orange) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of density in the axial channel and the co-elution of GFP-SsrA with ClpXP.

claim: The substrate enters ClpX at an angle of ~15° relative to the ClpP symmetry axis.
source: The substrate enters ClpX at an angle of ~15° relative to the ClpP symmetry axis and is gripped by five of the six ClpX protomers arranged in a right-handed spiral, akin to other AAA+ ATPases in their substrate-bound conformations (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017).
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structures and compared to other AAA+ ATPases.

claim: The substrate is gripped by five of the six ClpX protomers arranged in a right-handed spiral.
source: The substrate enters ClpX at an angle of ~15° relative to the ClpP symmetry axis and is gripped by five of the six ClpX protomers arranged in a right-handed spiral, akin to other AAA+ ATPases in their substrate-bound conformations (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Gates et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures and is consistent with other AAA+ ATPases.

claim: The sixth protomer forms a disengaged 'seam' that bridges protomers at the beginning and end of the spiral.
source: The sixth protomer forms a disengaged 'seam' that bridges protomers at the beginning and end of the spiral.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: In Conformation A, protomer X1 is disengaged from substrate and in the seam position.
source: In Conformation A, protomer X1 is disengaged from substrate and in the seam position (Figure 1F left - dark blue) while in Conformation B protomer X6 is disengaged from substrate and in the seam position (Figure 1F right - yellow).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In Conformation B, protomer X6 is disengaged from substrate and in the seam position.
source: In Conformation A, protomer X1 is disengaged from substrate and in the seam position (Figure 1F left - dark blue) while in Conformation B protomer X6 is disengaged from substrate and in the seam position (Figure 1F right - yellow).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In Conformation A the seam is in the 'upper seam' (US) position, further from the apical surface of ClpP.
source: However, these two seam positions are not equivalent: in Conformation A the seam is further from the apical surface of ClpP in what we designate as the 'upper seam' (US) position (Figure 1D,F - dark blue), while in Conformation B, the seam is closer to ClpP in the 'lower seam' (LS) position (Figure 1D,F - yellow).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: In Conformation B, the seam is in the 'lower seam' (LS) position, closer to ClpP.
source: However, these two seam positions are not equivalent: in Conformation A the seam is further from the apical surface of ClpP in what we designate as the 'upper seam' (US) position (Figure 1D,F - dark blue), while in Conformation B, the seam is closer to ClpP in the 'lower seam' (LS) position (Figure 1D,F - yellow).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: In both Conformations A and B, there is clear density for most of the IGF loops that extend from the ClpX ring toward the apical surface of ClpP.
source: In both Conformations A and B of ClpXP, there is clear density for most of the IGF loops that extend from the ClpX ring toward the apical surface of ClpP (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Conformation A, clear density is observed for only five of the six IGF loops, with weak density for the IGF loop of the X6 protomer.
source: In Conformation A, clear density is observed for only five of the six IGF loops, with weak density belonging to the IGF loop of the X6 protomer (white dotted line in Figure 2B left; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Conformation B, all six of the IGF loops are accounted for.
source: In Conformation B, the density of the X6 IGF loop is significantly stronger than in Conformation A, so that all six of the IGF loops are accounted for (residues 264–274, Figure 2B, right; Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with the loops binding six of the seven pockets on ClpP.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both Conformations A and B, the empty ClpP-binding pocket is located between the X5 and X6 protomers of ClpX.
source: In both Conformations A and B, the empty ClpP-binding pocket is located between the X5 and X6 protomers of ClpX (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lack of density for the IGF loop of protomer X6 in Conformation A is likely due to conformational flexibility and sub-stoichiometric binding of this IGF loop into the ClpP-binding pocket.
source: The lack of density for the IGF loop belonging to protomer X6 in Conformation A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) is likely due to conformational flexibility and sub-stoichiometric binding of this IGF loop into the ClpP-binding pocket.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak density observed in the cryo-EM maps.

claim: All six IGF loops in ClpX adopt different configurations in Conformations A and B.
source: All six IGF loops in ClpX adopt different configurations in Conformations A and B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ClpX residues immediately following where the IGF loops contact ClpP (residues 275–280) show weak or no density, likely indicating flexibility.
source: The ClpX residues immediately following where the IGF loops contact ClpP (residues 275–280) show weak or no density, likely indicating flexibility.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps and interpreted as flexibility.

claim: The flexibility of the IGF loops accommodates the spiral arrangement of ClpX necessary to bind and unfold substrate, while maintaining contact with the planar ring of ClpP.
source: In this way, the flexibility of the IGF loops accommodates the spiral arrangement of ClpX necessary to bind and unfold substrate, while maintaining contact with the planar ring of ClpP.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of IGF loop conformations.

claim: ClpX binding opens the N-terminal gates of ClpP.
source: Degradation assays (Effantin et al., 2010; Gribun et al., 2005; Martin et al., 2007; Ortega et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2000) show that ClpX allows substrate access to the degradation chamber of ClpP, suggesting that ClpX binding opens the N-terminal gates of ClpP.
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays cited in the text and confirmed by the structural data.

claim: In both Conformations A and B the gates are in the 'up' state, forming ordered β-hairpins.
source: Indeed, in both Conformations A and B the gates are in the 'up' state, forming ordered β-hairpins (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ClpP N-terminal β-hairpins closely resemble the conformation seen in ADEP-bound structures of NmClpP.
source: These β-hairpins closely resemble the conformation seen in the ADEP-bound structures of NmClpP (Goodreid et al., 2016) and are notably different from the disordered conformations observed in NmClpP when it is not bound to either ClpX or ADEP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Mabanglo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is determined by comparing the cryo-EM structure to published structures.

claim: ClpX binding creates a wide entrance pore with a diameter of ~23 Å for substrates to pass through into the ClpP degradation chamber.
source: By forming ordered gates, ClpX binding creates a wide entrance pore with a diameter of ~23 Å for substrates to pass through into the ClpP degradation chamber (Figure 2G, left; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The activating mechanism of ADEPs involves a disorder-to-order transition of the ClpP N-terminal gates.
source: While it has long been suspected that the activating mechanism of ADEPs involves a disorder-to-order transition of these gates (Li et al., 2010), this observation provides direct evidence that ClpX binding has the same effect.
evidence: This is stated as a long-suspected mechanism with a citation, and the current structures provide direct evidence.

claim: ClpX binding has the same effect as ADEP binding on the ClpP N-terminal gates, causing a disorder-to-order transition.
source: While it has long been suspected that the activating mechanism of ADEPs involves a disorder-to-order transition of these gates (Li et al., 2010), this observation provides direct evidence that ClpX binding has the same effect.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the ClpX-bound and apo ClpP structures.

claim: The rigidification of the ClpP N-terminal gates varies substantially between protomers in both Conformations A and B.
source: In both Conformations A and B, the rigidification of the ClpP N-terminal gates varies substantially between protomers.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps showing different levels of density for different gates.

claim: The N-terminal residues of the ClpP protomer that is not bound to an IGF loop have the weakest density, appearing to possess the most flexibility at the top of the β-hairpin.
source: At one extreme, the N-terminal residues of the ClpP protomer that is not bound to an IGF loop have the weakest density, appearing to possess the most flexibility at the top of the β-hairpin (Figure 2G center; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The N-terminal residues of the ClpP protomer proximal to the X5 ClpX protomer are held rigidly through contacts with the ATPase.
source: In contrast, the N-terminal residues of the ClpP protomer proximal to the X5 ClpX protomer, are held rigidly through contacts with the ATPase (Figure 2G right).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The interaction between the X5 protomer and ClpP N-terminal gate is mediated by a pair of α-helices from protomer X5 (residues 254–262 and 291–296) adjacent to the IGF loop, and by another X5 α-helix that precedes the pore-2 loop (residues 186–192).
source: This interaction is mediated by a pair of α-helices from protomer X5 (residues 254–262 and 291–296) adjacent to the IGF loop, and by another X5 α-helix that precedes the pore-2 loop (residues 186–192).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The three α-helices from X5 stabilize the β-hairpin structure of the ClpP N-terminal residues by interacting with Arg17 at the top of the hairpin.
source: The three α-helices stabilize the β-hairpin structure of the ClpP N-terminal residues by interacting with Arg17 at the top of the hairpin (Figure 2E inset).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The interactions between X5 and ClpP gates are unique for the X5 protomer due to the lateral displacement of the ClpX ring relative to the axial pore of ClpP.
source: These interactions are unique for the X5 protomer due to the lateral displacement of the ClpX ring relative to the axial pore of ClpP (Figure 2A), with the X2 protomer shifted furthest from the pore while the X5 protomer is pulled overtop of the pore (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figures 2A, 2D, and 2F.

claim: Gate rigidification appears to be mediated by an allosteric effect when IGF loops engage their respective ClpP binding pockets, akin to the effect observed upon ADEP binding.
source: Gate rigidification therefore appears to be mediated by an allosteric effect when IGF loops engage their respective ClpP binding pockets, akin to the effect observed upon ADEP binding (Gersch et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gates are rigidified even without direct contact with ClpX, and is compared to ADEP binding.

claim: In the ClpXP complex with substrate bound, only a single ClpX protomer (X5) interacts directly with a single ClpP gate at any given time.
source: In the ClpXP complex with substrate bound, only a single ClpX protomer (X5) interacts directly with a single ClpP gate at any given time.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The mechanism of substrate translocation involves movement of the ClpX ring on the apical surface of ClpP, with each ClpX protomer forming contacts with a ClpP gate as translocation proceeds.
source: The mechanism of substrate translocation described below involves movement of the ClpX ring on the apical surface of ClpP, with each ClpX protomer forming contacts with a ClpP gate as translocation proceeds.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and the proposed mechanism.

claim: ClpX fits into the emerging consensus for how AAA+ unfoldases engage substrate.
source: ClpX fits neatly into the emerging consensus for how AAA+ unfoldases engage substrate (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated by comparing ClpX to other AAA+ unfoldases with citations.

claim: In both Conformations A and B, five of the six pore-1 loops of ClpX interact tightly with the substrate backbone, with Tyr153 forming the majority of the interface.
source: In both Conformations A and B, five of the six pore-1 loops of ClpX interact tightly with the substrate backbone, with Tyr153 forming the majority of the interface (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Five protomers generate a right-handed spiral that wraps around an 8 to 10 residue stretch of the substrate along the central channel of ClpX.
source: These protomers generate a right-handed spiral that wraps around an 8 to 10 residue stretch of the substrate along the central channel of ClpX (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: In Conformation A, the X1 pore-1 loop in the US orientation is disengaged.
source: In Conformation A, the X1 pore-1 loop in the US orientation is disengaged, with the X2 protomer at the top of the spiral.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: In Conformation B, the X6 pore-1 loop is disengaged (LS orientation), while the X1 pore-1 loop engages a new section of substrate.
source: In Conformation B, the X6 pore-1 loop is disengaged (LS orientation), while the X1 pore-1 loop engages a new section of substrate (Figure 3D) and the X5 protomer is now located closest to the ClpP surface.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When transitioning between substrate-engaged and disengaged states, the X6 pore-1 loop undergoes a large conformational change.
source: When transitioning between substrate-engaged and disengaged states, the X6 pore-1 loop undergoes a large conformational change (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures in Figure 3E.

claim: As the X6 pore-1 loop disengages the substrate, the 'lasso' fold that allows Tyr153 and Val154 to point toward the substrate is replaced by a short α-helix immediately following the GYVG motif of the loop.
source: As it disengages the substrate the 'lasso' fold (Figure 3E, left) that allows Tyr153 and Val154 of pore-1 to point toward the substrate is replaced by a short α-helix immediately following the GYVG motif of the loop.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In Conformation B, the X1 and X5 protomers make additional contacts with the substrate.
source: Interestingly, the X1 and X5 protomers make additional contacts with the substrate in Conformation B.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: In Conformation B, the X1 protomer extends its pore-2 loop residues Ile198 and Thr199 to engage the substrate at a position three or four residues down the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds.
source: Whereas all of the pore-2 loops from the other five protomers are radially removed and disengaged from the substrate, the X1 protomer extends its pore-2 loop residues Ile198 and Thr199 to engage the substrate at a position three or four residues down the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: The RKH loops are conserved motifs among the ClpX family of AAA+ unfoldases and are known to contribute to substrate recognition.
source: The RKH loops, located at the top of the ClpX ring (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), are conserved motifs among the ClpX family of AAA+ unfoldases and are known to contribute to substrate recognition (Martin et al., 2007; Farrell et al., 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Conformation B, only the RKH loop of X5 directly engages substrate, with its His230 residue interacting at a position three or four residues up the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds.
source: In Conformation B, only the RKH loop of X5 directly engages substrate, with its His230 residue interacting at a position three or four residues up the substrate chain from where its pore-1 loop binds (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: In order to contact substrate, the RKH loop of the X5 protomer rearranges to point toward ClpP, in contrast to the other RKH loops that point away from the axial channel of ClpX.
source: In order to contact substrate at this position the RKH loop of the X5 protomer rearranges to point toward ClpP (Figure 3F), in contrast to the other RKH loops that point away from the axial channel of ClpX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The five RKH loops not contacting substrate are located away from the substrate and have weaker density in the maps, likely indicating flexibility.
source: These five RKH loops are located away from the substrate, and have weaker density in the maps, likely indicating flexibility.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps and interpreted as flexibility.

claim: The cryo-EM maps allowed unambiguous identification of the nucleotide bound to each ClpX protomer.
source: The cryo-EM maps allowed unambiguous identification of the nucleotide bound to each ClpX protomer.
evidence: This is stated based on the quality of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: In Conformation A, there is strong density for ATP and a magnesium cofactor in protomers X2, X3, X4, and X5.
source: In Conformation A, there is strong density for ATP and a magnesium cofactor in protomers X2, X3, X4, and X5, while the X1 and X6 protomers are ADP loaded, with no density for either the γ-phosphate or magnesium (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: In Conformation A, the X1 and X6 protomers are ADP loaded, with no density for either the γ-phosphate or magnesium.
source: In Conformation A, there is strong density for ATP and a magnesium cofactor in protomers X2, X3, X4, and X5, while the X1 and X6 protomers are ADP loaded, with no density for either the γ-phosphate or magnesium (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: The orientation between the large and the small AAA+ domains of ClpX changes considerably depending on the nucleotide state.
source: As in both the classic and HCLR clades of AAA+ ATPases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017), the orientation between the large and the small AAA+ domains of ClpX changes considerably depending on the nucleotide state.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures and is consistent with other AAA+ ATPases.

claim: In Conformation A, both the X1 and X6 protomers adopt conformations that allow the X1 protomer to move away from the pore in the US position.
source: In Conformation A, both the X1 and X6 protomers adopt conformations that allow the X1 protomer to move away from the pore in the US position (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and there is reduced surface area buried between X1 and its neighboring protomers X2 and X6.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The local resolution in the cryo-EM maps suggests that the X1 protomer in the US position is significantly more flexible than the other protomers.
source: In agreement with this finding, the local resolution in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggests that the X1 protomer in the US position is significantly more flexible than the other protomers.
evidence: This is observed in the local resolution maps shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Conformation B, only the X6 protomer is ADP-bound.
source: In Conformation B, only the X6 protomer is ADP-bound.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps.

claim: In Conformation B, the X1, X2, X3, X4, and X5 protomers are ATP-bound with clear density for the γ-phosphate and the magnesium cofactor.
source: The X1, X2, X3, X4, and X5 protomers are ATP-bound with clear density for the γ-phosphate and the magnesium cofactor (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM maps shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: The X5 protomer adopts a unique orientation between its large domain and small domain compared to the other ATP-bound protomers in order to accommodate the translation of the X6 protomer away from the substrate translocation channel into the LS position.
source: Interestingly, the X5 protomer adopts a unique orientation between its large domain and small domain compared to the other ATP-bound protomers in order to accommodate the translation of the X6 protomer away from the substrate translocation channel into the LS position (Figure 4B orange box; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Conformation A, the β- and γ-phosphates of the bound ATP are stabilized by interactions with the sensor-II arginine (Arg369) of the same subunit and the arginine finger (Arg306) from the adjacent clockwise protomer.
source: In Conformation A, the β- and γ-phosphates of the bound ATP are stabilized by interactions with the sensor-II arginine (Arg369) of the same subunit and the arginine finger (Arg306) from the adjacent clockwise protomer (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the ADP-bound sites of the X1 and X6 protomers in Conformation A, both arginines have moved away, allowing for a more open nucleotide-binding pocket.
source: In the ADP-bound sites of the X1 and X6 protomers, both arginines have moved away, allowing for a more open nucleotide-binding pocket (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Conformation B, both the sensor-II arginine and the arginine finger contact the β and γ-phosphates in only four of the five ATP-bound protomers (X1, X2, X3, and X4).
source: In Conformation B, both the sensor-II arginine and the arginine finger contact the β and γ-phosphates in only four of the five ATP-bound protomers (X1, X2, X3, and X4) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the X5 protomer of Conformation B, the adjacent X6 protomer and its arginine finger have pivoted away from the nucleotide into the LS position, allowing the sensor-II arginine to move closer to the γ-phosphate of the bound nucleotide.
source: In the X5 protomer (at the bottom of the spiral), the adjacent X6 protomer and its arginine finger have pivoted away from the nucleotide into the LS position, allowing the sensor-II arginine to move closer to the γ-phosphate of the bound nucleotide.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The resolution of the experimental map was not sufficient to differentiate between ATP and a long-lived post-hydrolysis ADP/Pi state in the X5 protomer of Conformation B.
source: While there is clear density for the γ-phosphate, the resolution of our experimental map was not sufficient to differentiate between ATP and a long-lived post-hydrolysis ADP/Pi state.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the resolution of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The sensor II-priming motif in the nucleotide site adjacent to an ADP bound site has also been reported for the Lon protease bound to substrate.
source: Notably, this key sensor II-priming motif in the nucleotide site adjacent to an ADP bound site has also been reported for the Lon protease bound to substrate (Shin et al., 2019), a close relative in the HCLR clade of AAA+ proteins.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Shin et al., 2019.

claim: Two distinct conformations of ClpX were identified, at 3.3 Å and 2.9 Å resolution, referred to as Conformations A and B, respectively.
source: Further local refinement and classification in cryoSPARC (Punjani et al., 2017) improved the density for ClpX and revealed two distinct conformations, at 3.3 Å and 2.9 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), hereafter referred to as Conformations A and B, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the image processing workflow.

claim: Focused refinement of ClpP with D7 symmetry enforced led to a map at 2.3 Å resolution.
source: Focused refinement of ClpP with D7 symmetry enforced led to a map at 2.3 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the image processing workflow.

claim: The transition from Conformation A to Conformation B involves X1 moving to the highest position of the spiral with respect to substrate and simultaneously exchanging ADP for ATP in its nucleotide-binding pocket.
source: In Conformation B, X1 moves to the highest position of the spiral with respect to substrate (compare Figure 2F, top and bottom panels) simultaneously exchanging ADP for ATP in its nucleotide-binding pocket (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5B and Figure 2F.

claim: The transition from Conformation A to Conformation B brings X1 into close proximity with X2 and allows engagement of X1's pore loops with substrate.
source: This transition brings X1 into close proximity with X2 and allows engagement of X1's pore loops with substrate.
evidence: This is described in the discussion as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The X1 pore-l loop sits at the top of the spiral, two substrate residues above the X2 pore loop in Conformation B.
source: The X1 pore-l loop now sits at the top of the spiral, two substrate residues above the X2 pore loop (Figure 5A and B), thereby translocating additional residues of substrate into the unfoldase.
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The transition from Conformation A to Conformation B leads to release of substrate by X6, which pivots away from the central pore to adopt the LS position.
source: This transition also leads to release of substrate by X6, which pivots away from the central pore to adopt the LS position (second ring, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release by X5 restores the ClpX spiral back to the Conformation A state.
source: ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release by X5, which was in the ATP-hydrolysis primed ATP* state, restores the ClpX spiral back to the Conformation A state, (third ring of the four in Figure 5A), with X6 now assuming the US position.
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Each Conformation A→Conformation B→Conformation A step results in the exchange of ADP for ATP and a single ATP hydrolysis event.
source: Each Conformation A→Conformation B→Conformation A step results in the exchange of ADP for ATP and a single ATP hydrolysis event.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Continuous repetition of the A→B→A steps leads to a processive 'hand-over-hand' translocation of substrate through the axial pore of ClpX into ClpP.
source: Continuous repetition of these steps leads to a processive 'hand-over-hand' translocation of substrate through the axial pore of ClpX into ClpP (Illustrated in Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Video 2.

claim: The sequential hydrolysis of ATP results in unidirectional substrate translocation and movement of pore loops along the substrate.
source: The sequential hydrolysis of ATP at the ATP* position results in unidirectional substrate translocation and movement of pore loops along the substrate (Figure 5B), with the counter clockwise hydrolysis cycle translating into a repeated downward pulling force on the substrate.
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Both the sequential hydrolysis of ATP as well as the 'hand-over-hand' substrate pulling model appear to be conserved for AAA+ unfoldases.
source: Both the sequential hydrolysis of ATP as well as the 'hand-over-hand' substrate pulling model appear to be conserved for AAA+ unfoldases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on other AAA+ unfoldases.

claim: Following ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release, the IGF loop of the protomer in the ATP* position must leave its engaged pocket and move to bind the adjacent empty site on ClpP.
source: Thus, following ATP hydrolysis and phosphate release, the IGF loop of the protomer in the ATP* position (X5 initially) must leave its engaged pocket and move to bind the adjacent empty site on ClpP (red arrows in Figure 5C), as the complex transitions back to Conformation A (third ring in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5C and Figure 5A.

claim: After seven IGF loop release and reengagement events, accompanied by seven ATP hydrolysis steps, the 'empty' ClpP binding site makes a complete cycle, returning to its starting position.
source: After seven IGF loop release and reengagement events, accompanied by seven ATP hydrolysis steps, the 'empty' ClpP binding site makes a complete cycle, returning to its starting position (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: Seven IGF loop transitions lead to a net 60° rotation of ClpX with respect to ClpP.
source: The accompanying motion of ClpX on the apical surface of ClpP for a given IGF loop transition is complex and subtle, yet seven of these transitions lead to a net 60° rotation of ClpX with respect to ClpP (note the positions of the purple ClpX protomer in the first and seventh panels in Figure 5D; Video 3).
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 5D and Video 3.

claim: The IGF loop of the X5 protomer has an 'extended/stretched' structure in the ATP* position of Conformation B, which likely causes strain and facilitates loop release and subsequent binding to the corresponding site on the adjacent ClpP protomer.
source: Consistent with this model, the IGF loop of the X5 protomer has an 'extended/stretched' structure in the ATP* position of Conformation B (Figure 2F), which likely causes strain and facilitates loop release and subsequent binding to the corresponding site on the adjacent ClpP protomer (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is described in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 2F and Figure 5C.

claim: During preparation of this manuscript, two manuscript preprints reported structures of ClpXP from L. monocytogenes and from E. coli.
source: During preparation of this manuscript, two manuscript preprints reported structures of ClpXP from L. monocytogenes (Gatsogiannis et al., 2019) and from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019), with ClpX resolutions ranging from 3.9 to 6 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to the preprints.

claim: In all species, the ClpX ring appears to adopt a similar offset relative to the symmetry axis of ClpP, indicating that the general architecture of the ClpXP machinery is conserved.
source: In all species, the ClpX ring appears to adopt a similar offset relative to the symmetry axis of ClpP, indicating that the general architecture of the ClpXP machinery is conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the NmClpXP structures to those from other species.

claim: The N-terminal apical loops of L. monocytogenes ClpP are not rigidified upon ClpX binding, in contrast to the observation in N. meningitidis that the gates rigidify upon binding.
source: Notably, however, the N-terminal apical loops of L. monocytogenes ClpP are not rigidified upon ClpX binding (Gatsogiannis et al., 2019), in contrast to the observation here that the gates rigidify upon binding to create a pore for substrate entry.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the NmClpXP structures to those from L. monocytogenes.

claim: Unusual head-to-head dimers of L. monocytogenes ClpXP were observed that appeared to be mediated by the zinc binding domains.
source: In the case of L. monocytogenes ClpXP, unusual head-to-head dimers were observed that appeared to be mediated by the zinc binding domains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to Gatsogiannis et al., 2019.

claim: Despite the presence of the zinc-binding domains in the N. meningitidis construct, no head-to-head dimers were observed.
source: Despite the presence of the zinc-binding domains in our N. meningitidis construct, no such dimers were observed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: The glutaraldehyde chemical crosslinker used to stabilize the L. monocytogenes ClpXP complex may have induced the formation of artefactual dimers.
source: While this difference may be due to differences across species, we note that the glutaraldehyde chemical crosslinker used to stabilize the L. monocytogenes ClpXP complex may have induced the formation of artefactual dimers.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the difference.

claim: Substrate engagement is different between the ClpXP from N. meningitidis and from E. coli.
source: Notably, substrate engagement is different between the ClpXP from N. meningitidis described here and from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the two structures.

claim: In N. meningitidis Conformation A, there is no engagement of substrate by any of the six pore-2 or six RKH loops.
source: In Conformation A seen with N. meningitidis, there is no engagement of substrate by any of the six pore-2 or six RKH loops, while in Conformation B only a single RKH loop and a single pore-2 loop contact substrate (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: In recently reported E. coli ClpXP structures, arginines located in the pore-2 loop from three to five different protomers, as well as multiple RKH loops, form major contacts with substrate.
source: This observation is in contrast to the recently reported E. coli ClpXP structures (Fei et al., 2019) in which arginines located in the pore-2 loop from three to five different protomers (depending on the structure), as well as multiple RKH loops, form major contacts with substrate.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Fei et al., 2019.

claim: The differences in substrate interactions may reflect that while pore-1 loop and RKH loop motifs are critical for forming interactions with substrate and providing the force for translocation, additional contacts may differ between species and may be necessary for recognition of degradation signals and for substrate specificity.
source: The differences in these interactions may reflect the fact that while pore-1 loop and RKH loop motifs are critical for forming interactions with substrate, and in the case of pore-1 loops in particular, in providing the force for translocation, additional contacts may differ between species and may be necessary for recognition of degradation signals and for substrate specificity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observed differences.

claim: The RKH loops are essential for the recognition of SsrA-tagged substrates by E. coli ClpX.
source: The RKH loops are essential for the recognition of SsrA-tagged substrates by E. coli ClpX, while human ClpX, which substitutes the RKH sequence with an RKL tripeptide and contains pore-1 loops with the same sequence as E. coli ClpX, fails to recognize substrates with the SsrA-tag.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: An engineered human ClpX construct bearing the pore-2 and RKH loops of E. coli ClpX is able to unfold SsrA-tagged substrates.
source: Notably, however, an engineered human construct bearing the pore-2 and RKH loops of E. coli ClpX is able to unfold SsrA-tagged substrates (Farrell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Farrell et al., 2007.

claim: Reordering of RKH loop residues to KHR and KRH results in significantly impaired substrate degradation.
source: Reordering of RKH loop residues to KHR and KRH results in significantly impaired substrate degradation (Fei et al., 2019) and a more disrupting AAA mutant does not support ClpP degradation of a SsrA-tagged substrate (Fei et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Fei et al., 2019.

claim: The single point mutation RKH to RKA results in loss of activity for both SsrA and λO tagged substrates.
source: Furthermore, the single point mutation RKH to RKA results in loss of activity for both SsrA and λO tagged substrates.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The tight contact between H230 and the substrate in the N. meningitidis ClpXP maps provides a structural basis for understanding mutagenesis results showing the importance of the RKH loop.
source: The tight contact between H230 and the substrate in our maps provides a structural basis for understanding these mutagenesis results.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural data in light of previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: In the ClpXP structures from E. coli, the ClpX ring adopts the same spiral staircase arrangement observed in many AAA+ ATPases, strongly supporting the 'hand-over-hand' mechanism of substrate translocation.
source: Although in the ClpXP structures from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019) the ClpX ring adopts the same spiral staircase arrangement observed in many AAA+ ATPases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Huang et al., 2016), strongly supporting the 'hand-over-hand' mechanism of substrate translocation, the authors of this work instead posit a stochastic mechanism (Fei et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2005) for the HCLR clade of ATPases based on the observation of only a single bound ADP in their structures.
evidence: This is stated with citations to the E. coli ClpXP structures and other AAA+ ATPases.

claim: The authors of the E. coli ClpXP work posit a stochastic mechanism for the HCLR clade of ATPases based on the observation of only a single bound ADP in their structures.
source: Although in the ClpXP structures from E. coli (Fei et al., 2019) the ClpX ring adopts the same spiral staircase arrangement observed in many AAA+ ATPases (Monroe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; De la Peña et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019; Ripstein et al., 2017; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Huang et al., 2016), strongly supporting the 'hand-over-hand' mechanism of substrate translocation, the authors of this work instead posit a stochastic mechanism (Fei et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2005) for the HCLR clade of ATPases based on the observation of only a single bound ADP in their structures.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Fei et al., 2019 and Martin et al., 2005.

claim: A stochastic model involving stochastic nucleotide hydrolysis appears inconsistent with the observations in N. meningitidis ClpXP, with those for the related Lon protease where two neighboring protomers are bound with ADP, and with a recent structural model for a substrate-bound E. coli ClpAP complex.
source: Such a model, involving stochastic nucleotide hydrolysis, appears inconsistent with the observations here, with those for the related Lon protease (Shin et al., 2019) where two neighboring protomers are bound with ADP, and with a recent structural model for a substrate-bound E. coli ClpAP complex showing that the unbinding and rebinding of flexible IGL loops is coupled to substrate translocation as each protomer makes its way from the bottom to the top of the spiral (Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Shin et al., 2019 and Lopez et al., 2019.

claim: The proposed mechanism for E. coli ClpAP is similar to the one suggested for N. meningitides ClpXP.
source: The proposed mechanism in that case is similar to the one suggested here for N. meningitides ClpXP.
evidence: This is stated comparing the mechanism proposed for ClpAP to the one proposed for ClpXP.

claim: The identification of two conformations in the N. meningitidis enzyme and observations of the bound nucleotides in each ClpX protomer leads to a simple model of cyclic hydrolysis that results in unidirectional substrate translocation.
source: The identification of two conformations in the N. meningitidis enzyme and observations of the bound nucleotides in each ClpX protomer leads to a simple model of cyclic hydrolysis that, in turn, results in unidirectional substrate translocation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural data.

claim: In the proposed model, the substrate is always gripped by multiple protomers, with only a single protomer disengaged as it traverses from the bottom to the top of the spiral.
source: In this model, the substrate is always gripped by multiple protomers, with only a single protomer disengaged as it traverses from the bottom to the top of the spiral.
evidence: This is stated as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: While unique features will undoubtedly continue to emerge regarding subtle functional aspects of different AAA+ unfoldases, it is likely that the translocating forces generated by these molecular machines are based on a common mechanism.
source: While unique features will undoubtedly continue to emerge regarding subtle functional aspects of different AAA+ unfoldases it is likely that the translocating forces generated by these molecular machines are based on a common mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a general conclusion about AAA+ unfoldases.
